subject: Career
title: Why People Change Careers
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Why People Change Careers.

hook.text: The average person changes careers — not jobs, careers — three to seven times in their lifetime.

buildup.text: Technology, burnout, curiosity, and life events push people to reinvent professionally.

discovery.text: A Bureau of Labor Statistics study found workers hold an average of 12.4 jobs before age 55.

twist.text: Yet society still expects a linear path: study one thing, do it forever. The data says otherwise.

climax.text: Career changes aren't failures. They're adaptations to a world that never stops shifting.

punchline.text: The straight career path is the exception, not the rule.

quiz.question: How many times does the average person change careers in a lifetime?

details.summary: People switch careers for reasons ranging from burnout and misalignment of values to emerging opportunities and life changes. Research shows the average person changes careers three to seven times in a lifetime, and the trend is accelerating.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the drivers behind career changes helps you separate impulsive dissatisfaction from a genuine need for reinvention, saving years of indecision.
takeaways: Value misalignment is the top long-term trigger for career change
External shocks like layoffs often accelerate latent desires
Proactive changers report higher satisfaction than reactive ones

faq.question: Is changing careers multiple times seen as a red flag by employers?
faq.answer: Increasingly, no. Hiring managers value diverse experience when the candidate can articulate a coherent narrative linking each move. What matters is demonstrating growth and transferable skills rather than tenure alone.

faq.question: How do you know the urge to change careers is real and not just burnout?
faq.answer: Burnout usually fades after rest and boundary setting, while genuine career misalignment persists regardless of improved conditions. If the dissatisfaction remains after a sabbatical or reduced workload, it likely signals a deeper need for change.
